BLUE MOUNTAINS BIODIVERSITY ) Integrated Invasive Plant Management
PROJECT )
) Affirmed
ORDER
Blue Mountains Biodiversity Project (BMBP) appealed and petitioned to stay the
effect of a December 22, 2016, decision issued by the District Manager of the Bureau of
Land Management’s Vale District in Oregon (BLM). In the decision, BLM approved the
Integrated Invasive Plant Management Plan for the Vale District (Plan), which expands
the District’s noxious weeds program to include all invasive plants and increases the
number of herbicides that may be used from four to 17.
BMBP alleges that BLM’s decision to approve the Plan violates numerous laws and
policies. For example, it argues that BLM violated the National Environmental Policy Act
(NEPA), Endangered Species Act (ESA), and Clean Water Act (CWA). It also argues that
BLM’s Plan is in contravention of laws and policies related to special areas, including
Wilderness Areas, Wilderness Study Areas (WSAs), and Areas of Critical Environmental
Concern (ACECs), as well as special status and other plant and animal species. As we
explain below, BMBP’s arguments are primarily conclusory and unsupported, and
therefore are insufficient to show error in BLM’s decision. Accordingly, we affirm BLM’s
approval of the Plan.
A. BLM’s Decision to Approve thBeA InCtKeGgRraOtUedN IDn vasive Plant Management Plan
The Plan governs BLM’s efforts to control invasive plants in the Vale District, which
encompasses approximately five million acres in eastern Oregon and southeast

are “nonnative aggressive plants with the potential to cause significant damage to native
ecosystems and/or cause significant economic losses,” and noxious weeds, which “are a
subset of invasive plants that are county-, State-, or federally-listed as injurious to public
2

District, 50 species of terrestrial and aquatic invasive plants occupy over 197,781 acres in
over 27,500 separate known locations, and “noxious weeds are continuing to spread at an
3

Prior to adopting its Plan, the Vale District controlled noxious weeds using a range
of methods, including manual and mechanical methods, biological control agents (mostly
4

BLM identified several factors demonstrating the need to consider an expanded integrated
invasive plant management plan for the Vale District, including the continued spread of
noxious weeds, widespread ecological damage caused by invasive plants, and the existence
of newer and more species-specific herbicides that could be used in lower quantities and
5

B. BMBP Has Not Demonstrated that BLM Violated NEPA
BMBP asserts that BLM violated various provisions of NEPA and its implementing
31
regulations in approving the Plan. BMBP makes five major arguments: (1) BLM erred by
not preparing an EIS, (2) BLM used an overly narrow purpose and need that unlawfully
constrained the alternatives considered; (3) BLM failed to analyze a reasonable range of
alternatives; (4) BLM failed to take a hard look at the direct, indirect, and cumulative effects
32
of the Plan; and (5) BLM failed to use the best available science. After setting out the
standard of review and burden of proof, we address each of these allegations.
1. Standard of review and burden of proof governing challenges to EAs
NEPA requires Federal agencies to prepare an EIS evaluating the potential
environmental impacts of major Federal actions significantly affecting the quality of the
33
human environment. Agencies may prepare an EA to determine whether an EIS is
34
required or to aid the agency’s decision-making when an EIS is not necessary. An EA is a
“concise public document” that includes a brief discussion of the need for the proposed
action, alternatives to the action, the environmental impacts of the proposed action and
alternatives, and a listing of agencies and persons consulted during the preparation of the
35
EA. The level of detail and depth of impact analysis in an EA is appropriately limited to
the minimum needed to dneotetrmine whether there would be significant environmental
36
impacts from the proposed action. Consequently, an EA “is intended to be an overview of
environmental concerns, an exhaustive study of all environmental issues which the

The Board is guided by a “rule of reason” in assessing an EA’s adequacy. The Board
will find an EA adequate if the record demonstrates that BLM has considered all relevant
matters of environmental concern, taken a “hard look” at potential environmental impacts,
and made a convincing case that no significant impact will result or that any such impact

have explained that “the Board’s role is not to decide if an [EA] is based upon the best
scientific data and methodology available . . . , but rather to determine whether BLM’s

An appellant challenging the adequacy of an EA has the burden of demonstrating

2. BLM was not required to prepare an EIS
BLM must prepare an EIS for major Federal actions significantly affecting the quality
46
of the human environment. Under the regulations implementing NEPA, significance is
determined by considering both context (for example, the effects on the locale of the
47
proposed action) and intensity (the severity of impacts). The regulations list several
considerations important to the evaluation of intensity, including “[t]he degree to which
48
the effects on the quality of the human environment are likely to be highly controversial”
and “[t]he degree to which the possible effects on the human environment are highly
49
uncertain or involve unique or unknown risks.”
BMBP asserts that BLM did not appropriately evaluate these two intensity
considerations, stating that BLM should have prepared an EIS based on the large scale of
the Plan (over 5 million acres), “broader public concern over toxic herbicide use,” and
50
“substantial scientific uncertainties as to herbicide effects.” But BMBP cites no support for
its assertion, simply repeating its comments on the draft EAs, and does not meet its burden
to show error in BLM’s decision to prepare an EA.
First, under NEPA, controversy does not exist because people oppose a proposed
action. Rather, controversy exists when there is a scientific dispute about the size, nature,
51
or effect of a proposed action. Simply stated, controversy concerns the effects of the
52
proposed action, not the proposed action itself. BMBP’s general assertion of a “broader
public concern” does not demonstrate the existence of actual controversy with respect to
the environmental effects of the Plan. Moreover, BLM assessed each of the intensity factors
and concluded that the effects of the Plan would not be highly controversial, especially in
light of the extensive and up-to-date testing and study of the human health and ecological

61
“considerable discretion” to define the purpose and need of a project. We review BLM’s
62
exercise of this discretion under a “rule of reason.”
Here, BLM defined the purpose and need for the proposed action in terms of
addressing the spread of invasive plant species through an expanded list of herbicides
available for BLM’s use. BLM’s stated need highlighted that: invasive plants were
continuing to spread in the district; some invasive plant species could not be effectively
controlled by the four herbicides approved for use under the existing program; newer,
more species-specific herbicides that could be used in lower quantities and that pose less
environmental risk were not approved for use under the existing program; and BLM’s
inability to use herbicides commonly used by cooperators on adjacent lands hampered
63
cooperative public/private invasive plant control efforts. BLM’s stated purpose of the
proposed action was to “[c]ontrol invasive plants to protect native ecosystems and the flora
and fauna that depend on them,” “[m]anage invasive plants to reduce the risk that large-
scale high-intensity fires would unacceptably damage resources and human
developments,” “[c]ooperatively control invasive plants so they do not infest or re-infest
adjacent non-BLM-administered lands, “[p]revent control treatments from having
unacceptable adverse effects to applicators and the public, to desirable flora and fauna, and
to soil, air, and water,” and “[m]inimize treatment costs and improve treatment
64
effectiveness.”

preventing treatments from having unacceptable adverse effects and instead, emphasizes
65

BLM explained in the record why it focused on herbicide use. BLM stated that
mechanical treatments, favored by BMBP, “are typically non-selective, and remove or
damage target and non-target plants alike,” and “have limited use for noxious weed control
69
unless coupled with other treatments.” BLM thus focused on an expanded list of
herbicides, explaining that the use of more selective herbicides could more effectively
control certain invasive species and having more herbicides available for use would help
prevent herbicide resistance by adding chemicals that control the plants through different
70

would continue to slow the spread of noxious weeds within the District, but “certain
71
noxious weeds and most of the other invasive plants would continue to spread.” The
record thus shows that BLM had a rational basis for its decision to focus on additional
herbicides in defining its purpose and need.
We conclude that BLM reasonably used its discretion to define the purpose and
need for its proposed action by identifying, among other things, the spread of invasive
plants; the availability of newer, more species-specific herbicides; and the risk to BLM-
managed lands and resources without expansion of the herbicides available for use.
BMBP’s argument that BLM’s purpose and need was unreasonably constrained by focusing
on “excessive herbicide use” is unsupported, and BMBP’s preference that BLM focus on
control methods other than herbicide use amounts to a mere difference of opinion, which

4. BLM analyzed an appropriate range of alternatives
Related to its claim that BLM’s purpose and need statement was overly narrow,
73
BMBP argues that the EA did not analyze a reasonable range of alternatives. BMBP states
that BLM should have considered additional alternatives, including an alternative
prohibiting all herbicide use; an alternative prohibiting aerial spraying of herbicides; an
alternative using fewer herbicides; and an alternative allowing herbicide use only after
74
non-herbicide methods are used. Although BMBP acknowledges that BLM explained in its
EA that it eliminated these alternatives from detailed analysis, BMBP repeats comments it
made on the draft EAs asserting that these alternatives should be considered, and further
states that the revised proposed action “still includes unnecessary continued use of highly
toxic, persistent, and non-selective herbicides with significant ecological and human health
75
impacts that could be replaced by other control methods and less harmful herbicides.”
We find that BLM analyzed an appropriate range of alternatives in its EA, in
compliance with NEPA. In its revised final EA, BLM analyzed a no action alternative, the
